newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's Kuchma to press G7 on Chernobyl tomb.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's Kuchma to press G7 on Chernobyl tomb.

text.p: President Leonid Kuchma said on Thursday that uncertainty over the state of the Chernobyl nuclear power station's ruined fourth reactor meant Ukraine had to press the West to help it build a new "tomb" around it.

"We must solve this problem. The next meeting with G7 (Group of Seven) is scheduled for October 8 and we will be more decisive about the necessity of building a new sarcophagus," Kuchma told reporters in southern Ukraine.
Kuchma was speaking after reports that higher neutron radiation readings last week in the existing "sarcophagus" around the fourth reactor of the infamous nuclear station could cause a new explosion.
Experts from the G7 wealthy countries hold their next regular meeting with Ukrainian officials in Paris on how to finance Ukraine's promise to shut Chernobyl's two working reactors by the year 2000.
The G7 has pledged more than $3 billion in grants and credits but Ukraine says the money is too slow in coming. A proposal to build a new sarcophagus has made little progress.
Kuchma, speaking to reporters on Thursday, acknowledged that public opinion had been deeply affected by the recent reports on high neutron radiation readings.
Official attempts to ease public concern appear to have had little effect.
"You must not upset people in this way. I know this from my own family. At home people are asking me about this too," Kuchma said.
Despite a flurry of top-level statements that the sarcophagus posed no danger, Ukrainian and Russian media speculated on whether the ruined reactor could explode again.
Some commentators suggested Ukraine was exploiting the higher readings to secure more Western funds to close the plant -- site of the world's biggest nuclear accident in 1986.
"Is a new explosion brewing under the sarcophagus?" ran a headline in the daily Vseukrainsky Vedomosti.
Russia's top liberal daily Izvestia was far blunter.
"Nuclear blackmail for their own ends?" it asked in a front-page headline. "Kiev is again using Chernobyl to intimidate the world but specialists see no real danger."

Kuchma singled out for criticism Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko, who said this week that the higher readings had been caused by rain seeping through the 1,000 square metres of cracks in the tomb and amounted to a limited nuclear reaction.

"Anyone making such statements, particularly a member of the government, must accept responsibility for them," he said. "No one knows what sort of reactions are occurring in the sarcophagus. There are no specialists on this."
The State Nuclear authority, Derzhkomatom, issued a statement denying "any suggestion that the containment structure is on the brink of an accident".
Its chairman Viktor Chebrov said a commission investigating the higher readings had found no proof of a chain reaction. But he stressed a new structure had to be built.

Russian nuclear experts also said they saw no danger from the increases. A senior official of Russia's Nuclear Energy Ministry told Interfax news agency that measuring equipment inside the "tomb" was too old to give reliable readings.
Western experts said the levels were far below anything which could provoke a new explosion.
